channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: France's beet industry warned its 2026 sugar harvest could fall 20% below the five-year average after severe drought, a rare tornado injured 41 people in the Aude, and typhoons and floods again battered China and Taiwan.
item.description:
Extreme weather kept hitting agriculture and infrastructure across several regions. France's beet growers said conditions since spring have cut plants' growth potential through water stress and encouraged pests, so 2026 sugar output could run 20% below the five-year average, dragging down sugar, alcohol and bioethanol production, with neighbouring producers likely affected too. On 24 August a rare tornado struck Pomas in the Aude in south-west France, injuring 41 people and damaging about 300 of the village's 500 houses, forcing a full evacuation. In Germany, Chancellor Merz promised "concrete consequences" from the summer heatwave and drought. In Asia, China activated flood emergency responses across Beijing, Hebei, Fujian and Guangxi — where Typhoon Narra and heavy rain drove 14 rivers past warning levels and forced tens of thousands to evacuate — while Taiwan and southern Japan braced for Typhoon Saudel, which threatened to disrupt regional flights.

Industry Impact

The direct ACS exposure here is limited, but the second-order effects matter. Recurring drought and flooding across Europe and Asia disrupt agriculture, logistics and construction activity, and bio-based feedstock streams — France's beet-derived bioethanol among them — that some chemical and coatings inputs draw on. Physical-climate disruption is becoming a persistent supply-chain and demand variable rather than a one-off, affecting river transport, plant operations and raw-material availability across the regions where ACS producers and their customers operate. The practical read is to keep monitoring climate-driven risk to logistics and agricultural feedstocks as a standing item, especially where operations depend on European inland waterways or Asian coastal manufacturing hubs.

Reussir | Le Parisien | China Daily | People's Daily Online

item.title: International oil prices fell about 4% on 25 August as markets judged the new Iran sanctions milder than feared, and the IMF said the global economy has weathered the Iran-war energy shock better than expected despite mounting fiscal risks.
item.description:
The market response to the sanctions was relief, not alarm. Brent crude for October delivery fell about 3.9% to USD 88.58 a barrel and US WTI about 3.1% to USD 82.36 on 25 August, with both slipping further after the close, as traders concluded the "Operation Economic Outcast" package (covered in the sanctions insight in this alert) posed little direct threat to global supply and Washington had delayed some measures. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said the world economy had absorbed the energy shock better than feared — helped by releases of oil and gas reserves, softer demand and expanding renewables — describing a "tug of war" between the energy crisis and an AI-driven investment boom. She cautioned that risks are more balanced than in April but still tilt down, citing rising bond yields and stalled disinflation. A structural warning underlies the calm: Reuters/IEA data show over 43% of world oil supply — about 45 million barrels a day — now comes from countries hit by war, attacks or export curbs.

Industry Impact

Oil and gas are the feedstock and energy base beneath adhesives, coatings and sealants, so a roughly 4% price fall is a modest, welcome easing of input-cost pressure for chemical and ACS producers, and the IMF's resilience message reduces the near-term risk of a demand shock. The relief is fragile rather than structural: with more than 43% of global supply exposed to conflict, any escalation in the Gulf, Russia or elsewhere could reverse the move quickly, and fiscal strain plus sticky inflation could keep financing costs high. The practical read is to treat lower crude as a short-term margin tailwind while keeping feedstock-price hedging and scenario planning geared to renewed volatility.

The Straits Times | China Economic Net | Handelsblatt | The Times of India

item.title: India's economic growth is estimated to have cooled to about 7.1% in the April–June quarter from 7.8%, yet the Reserve Bank of India and industry bodies point to resilient manufacturing, services and domestic demand behind the slowdown.
item.description:
India's momentum eased but stayed among the world's fastest. A Reuters poll of economists put June-quarter growth at about 7.1%, down from 7.8% the previous quarter, supported by government and consumer spending while private investment stayed subdued and rising oil prices posed a household-budget risk; the Reserve Bank of India is expected to hold rates for six months. The RBI's own bulletin argued the economy shows "notable resilience" to global headwinds, citing rising manufacturing and services activity and buoyant domestic demand, with a recovering monsoon aiding crop sowing even as headline inflation edged above target on supply-side pressures. Context on scale: the IMF puts India's nominal GDP at USD 3.92 trillion for 2025–26, the world's sixth largest, and a new Confederation of Indian Industry report ("Champions and Challengers") assessed the competitiveness of strategic manufacturing sectors such as bearings, tyres and wearables to map where India can move up global value chains.

Industry Impact

India remains a structural growth market for chemicals and ACS, tied to construction, automotive, packaging and electronics demand that a ~7.1% expansion still supports. The cooling is a moderation, not a downturn, and the RBI's resilience message plus India's manufacturing-competitiveness drive point to durable medium-term demand for adhesives, sealants and coatings. The near-term watch-items are subdued private investment, which can delay industrial and infrastructure projects, and oil-linked input-cost and inflation risk. For ACS suppliers, India is best treated as a build-out market where local manufacturing capability and cost position increasingly matter, in line with the "Make in India" competitiveness agenda.

The Economic Times | Business Standard | The Hindu Business Line | CII

item.title: Taiwan's industrial production index hit a record 145.24 in July, up 25.6% year-on-year on AI chip and server demand, while Samsung and SK hynix moved to expand NAND memory-chip capacity at their plants in mainland China.
item.description:
The semiconductor cycle stayed strong and geographically mobile. Taiwan's Ministry of Economic Affairs said its July industrial production index reached a record 145.24, up 25.6% year-on-year — a 29th straight month of growth — with manufacturing at a record 147.65, driven by artificial-intelligence demand for wafer foundry, DRAM and AI servers. In China, SK hynix and Samsung are expanding their NAND flash bases: SK hynix plans capacity of 30,000 wafers a month from late 2026 into 2027 at its Dalian plant, while Samsung is converting its Xi'an line to advanced V9 NAND at 40,000–50,000 wafers a month. (NAND flash is the memory used in phones, SSDs and data-centre storage.) The two developments show AI demand lifting output in Taiwan while the Korean majors keep investing inside China despite US export-control pressure.

Industry Impact

Electronics and semiconductors are a specialised but high-value ACS end-market, using die-attach and underfill adhesives, encapsulants, conformal and protective coatings, and thermal-interface materials. Record Taiwanese output and continued NAND investment in China signal firm near-term demand for these electronic chemistries and for the materials used to build and equip fabs. The concentration of capacity in Taiwan and mainland China also reinforces a supply-chain dependency and a geopolitical-risk axis — export controls, cross-strait tension and US–China friction — that ACS suppliers to the electronics sector must factor into sourcing and customer exposure. The signal is demand-positive but tied tightly to the AI investment cycle and to trade-policy risk.

Commercial Times | Commercial Times | Silicon Saxony

item.title: China proposed letting resident individuals invest abroad with approval for the first time, and a revised Road Traffic Safety Law would make manufacturers liable for violations committed while a vehicle's autonomous-driving function is active.
item.description:
Beijing advanced two notable regulatory changes. The National Development and Reform Commission published a draft revision of its outbound-investment rules, open for comment until 20 September, that for the first time sets out how resident individuals — not just companies — can apply to approve or register foreign investment, with annual reporting and stricter disclosure of adverse events and overseas reinvestment. Separately, the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress reviewed a revised Road Traffic Safety Law on 25 August that adds a dedicated chapter on autonomous vehicles: it defines autonomous versus driver-assistance functions, requires compulsory accident-liability insurance, obliges makers and importers to ensure road, network and data safety, and bars exaggerated marketing of self-driving. Critically, when a violation occurs while the autonomous function is active, the manufacturer or importer — not the driver — is held responsible; vehicles with the function switched off, or with only assistance features, stay under existing rules.

Industry Impact

The autonomous-vehicle liability rules matter most to ACS producers through the automotive channel. Shifting accountability to manufacturers for active self-driving raises the stakes on component reliability and durability — including the structural adhesives, sensor-bonding and sealing, and protective coatings around cameras, radar and battery systems — and pushes carmakers toward higher-specification, better-documented materials. Clear national rules also reduce regulatory uncertainty, which tends to accelerate autonomous-vehicle rollout and the specialty-materials demand that comes with it. The outbound-investment opening is a lower-immediacy signal but points to gradually freer Chinese capital flows abroad, worth watching for its effect on cross-border investment and competition.

Lianhe Zaobao | South China Morning Post | Xinhua

item.title: China's humanoid-robot boom cooled sharply as Unitree lost about USD 30 billion in market value within three days of listing, even as Beijing's robot conferences showcased a national push into "embodied intelligence" and the sector's revenue grew 24.5%.
item.description:
The robotics story gained a reality check without losing momentum. Unitree Robotics, which listed on 19 August, saw its shares spike from a CNY 150 issue price to as high as CNY 1,100 before falling to CNY 603 by 22 August — a swing that briefly valued it near USD 66 billion and then erased about USD 30 billion, prompting questions about whether the AI-and-robotics craze has outrun fundamentals. The policy backdrop is expansionary: Beijing's World Robot Conference (373 firms, 3,000-plus products) and the second World Humanoid Robot Games (2,056 robots from 16 countries) framed a shift in the US–China AI contest from large language models to "embodied intelligence" — AI that perceives its surroundings, follows instructions and acts physically, tested here on wiring, logistics and industrial tasks. Officials reported robotics-sector revenue of CNY 165.5 billion in the first half, up 24.5%, and named intelligent robots a pillar industry. Separately, a US FCC ban on Chinese-made robots is hurting US startups that rely on cheap Chinese components.

Industry Impact

Industrial robotics and automation are a growing, ACS-relevant end-market: humanoid and service robots use structural adhesives, thermal and electronic potting compounds, sealants and specialty coatings, and rapid Chinese scale-up expands that demand pool — mostly inside China and mostly served by local formulators. The Unitree valuation swing is a caution that some of this demand is running ahead of real deployment, so ACS suppliers should size the opportunity on shipment and revenue data (up 24.5%) rather than share prices. The FCC component bottleneck also underlines how tightly the robotics supply chain — components and the chemistries around them — is concentrated in China, a strategic dependency for Western robotics and their materials suppliers alike.

Commercial Times | Chinatimes | Chinatimes | Chinatimes

item.title: US new single-family home sales fell 10.5% in July to a seven-month low of 607,000 units and the median price slipped to a four-year low, while Federal Reserve minutes showed four regional banks had pushed for a rate rise before July's hold.
item.description:
The US housing signal weakened. The Census Bureau said sales of new single-family homes fell 10.5% month-on-month (and about 6.3% year-on-year) to a seasonally adjusted 607,000 units in July, the lowest since January, with inventory rising to 9.6 months of supply — above the 7–8 months seen as balanced — and the median new-home price down 0.9% year-on-year to USD 393,800, a four-year low. Prices for existing homes told a different story: the S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller 20-city index rose 2.1% year-on-year in June, led by Chicago, New York and Cleveland. Separately, minutes showed directors at four of the Fed's twelve regional banks — Dallas, Cleveland, Minneapolis and Kansas City — wanted to raise the discount rate before the late-July meeting, where policymakers ultimately held the policy rate in a 9–3 vote. High financing costs remain the drag on new-build demand.

Industry Impact

US residential construction is a major end-market for adhesives, sealants and architectural and decorative coatings, so a 10.5% drop in new-home sales and rising unsold inventory point to softer near-term volumes for building-products formulators exposed to the US. Falling new-home prices squeeze builder margins and can delay project starts, while the Fed's reluctance to cut — with several regional banks even favouring a hike — signals that the high-rate environment weighing on construction is unlikely to ease quickly. The read for ACS suppliers is defensive on US new-build demand into late 2026, with repair-and-remodel and non-residential work the segments to watch for offsetting strength.

MarketScreener | Commercial Times | Dünya Gazetesi | MarketScreener

item.title: The EU's Industrial Accelerator Act, with low-carbon public-procurement quotas and "Made in Europe" content rules, enters a decisive autumn negotiation that pits France against Germany, even as member states keep the right to tax energy windfall profits.
item.description:
Europe's flagship green-industry policy is entering its hardest phase. The Industrial Accelerator Act — the centrepiece of Commission President von der Leyen's second term — would stimulate lower-carbon manufacturing by requiring public buyers to meet low-carbon procurement quotas and by adding "Made in Europe" content rules, aiming to create guaranteed demand for cleaner technologies. Politico reports the autumn talks over the final text will expose a France–Germany split over how far to go and how protectionist the local-content rules should be. In parallel, the EU confirmed that taxing energy companies' windfall profits remains a national competence: finance ministers from Germany, Italy, Austria, Poland, Portugal and Spain had asked for an EU-level levy, but the absence of a common framework leaves each country to act alone, raising regulatory uncertainty for utilities and energy-intensive sectors.

Industry Impact

The Act matters to ACS producers on both the cost and the demand side. Low-carbon procurement quotas and "Made in Europe" rules could create preferential demand for coatings, adhesives and sealants used in cleaner construction and manufacturing — but only for suppliers that can document low embodied carbon and European content, turning product carbon footprints into a market-access requirement. The France–Germany dispute signals the final rules are still fluid, so the compliance bar and timing are uncertain. The patchwork on windfall-profit taxes adds another variable to European energy costs, a core input for chemical makers. ACS suppliers should track the procurement-quota and content thresholds and start preparing carbon-footprint documentation for their European ranges.

Politico Europe | Il Sole 24 Ore

item.title: China now accounts for about 30% of global industrial production, up from around 5% in 2001, and Apollo's chief economist warns of a "China Shock 2.0" as Chinese high-tech exports surge and semiconductor shipments double.
item.description:
Two data points sharpen a structural story. Les Echos, citing production data, notes China's share of world industrial output has risen from just over 5% when it joined the World Trade Organization in 2001 to about 30% today, and on current trends could approach half of global production by the mid-2030s. Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Slok argues a "China Shock 2.0" is under way: unlike the 2000s wave of cheap consumer goods, this one is in high-value products such as semiconductors and electric vehicles that compete directly with Western firms. Chinese exports rose about 24% in July, high-tech exports climbed roughly 41% year-on-year in the first seven months, and semiconductor exports doubled. Domestically, Beijing says "new drivers" — high-end manufacturing and the digital economy — contributed more than half of industrial growth in January–July, and the State Council issued guidance to pair "China Service" with advanced manufacturing. The IMF projects 4.6% Chinese growth for 2026.

Industry Impact

For the chemical and ACS sector this reframes China from a low-cost source to a high-tech competitor and a demand engine at once. As China moves up the value chain in vehicles, electronics and machinery — all major ACS end-markets — its manufacturers increasingly localise the adhesives, coatings and specialty chemicals that Western suppliers once exported, squeezing volumes even where consumers are shielded by tariffs. At the same time, a China producing 30% of the world's goods remains the single largest market for industrial ACS inputs. The strategic read is to defend high-value, formulation-differentiated positions where localisation is hardest, and to treat rising Chinese high-tech export share as a structural driver of both competitive pressure and trade-defence risk in Western markets.

Les Echos | Fortune | China Economic Net | China Daily

item.title: The US launched "Operation Economic Outcast" against Iran, sanctioning about 60 targets that now include four Indian firms and dozens of Chinese and Hong Kong intermediaries, while again sparing Chinese banks as Tehran threatened the Gulf.
item.description:
Washington gave its Iran campaign a name and a wider reach. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said "Operation Economic Outcast" aims to sever Iran's financial networks worldwide, and the Office of Foreign Assets Control designated close to 60 people, entities and vessels across China, the UAE, Singapore, Switzerland and Europe accused of moving Iranian oil, funds and sensitive technology. For the first time the net directly caught four India-based traders and three nationals — including Sadashiva Overseas and Portease Partners — over roughly USD 119 million of Iranian petroleum and petrochemical imports, alongside dozens of Chinese and Hong Kong intermediaries and shadow-fleet operators, echoing the pattern of Russia-sanctions enforcement. Crucially, the package again avoided the large Chinese banks suspected of handling Iran's oil trade, and gave countries defined windows to cut ties rather than imposing the harshest penalties at once. Tehran vowed to retaliate, said China and Russia reject the move, and threatened to halt Gulf oil exports and treat support for sanctions as "an act of war"; the US is pairing the sanctions with a naval blockade.

Industry Impact

For ACS producers the lasting exposure here is compliance rather than immediate feedstock cost. By reaching intermediaries in India, China, Hong Kong, Singapore and the UAE, the campaign shows any customer, supplier, insurer or shipping partner with Iran links can be placed off-limits on a defined timeline, so counterparty screening and contract clauses need tightening across Asian and Gulf trade lanes. The decision to spare Chinese banks lowers the odds of an immediate US–China rupture over enforcement, but keeps that risk live for firms exposed to both markets. The muted oil reaction (see the oil and IMF insight in this alert) means the petrochemical-input channel is, for now, a smaller worry than the sanctions-compliance one.

The Economic Times | Global Times | Challenges | Business Standard | Hong Kong Economic Times

item.title: Germany's June construction orders rose 11.3% year-on-year and real sales 6.6%, and second-quarter GDP was revised up to 0.3%, as Chancellor Merz opened a cabinet retreat vowing to lead the economy "into a new era" of reform.
item.description:
Germany's core signals turned more positive. The Federal Statistical Office reported that new orders in the main construction industry rose 11.3% year-on-year in June 2026 (price- and calendar-adjusted) and real sales 6.6%, with growth in both building and civil engineering and employment up 1.5%; building permits rose more than 15% in the first half, the strongest since 2016. Separately, second-quarter GDP was revised up to 0.3% quarter-on-quarter from a first estimate of 0.2%, helped by stronger exports and trade — a sign the economy is handling the Iran-war energy shock better than feared. The tone is not uniformly upbeat: the construction association still cut its 2026 real revenue forecast to +1% (from 2.5%) on high costs and weak residential building, and the mid-sized builders' body BVMB pressed Berlin to deliver its promised EUR 169 billion for roads, rail and waterways. At a two-day cabinet retreat, Merz said he would push reform on growth, innovation and modernisation.

Industry Impact

Germany is the core European market for industrial adhesives, coatings and sealants, and construction is one of the largest ACS end-markets, so an 11.3% order jump and 15%-plus permit growth point to genuine near-term demand upside for building adhesives, sealants and architectural coatings. The signal is mixed rather than a boom: the revenue-forecast cut and weak residential segment show high costs still bite, and infrastructure demand depends on Berlin actually releasing the promised EUR 169 billion. The practical read is cautiously constructive — treat the order and permit data as the leading indicator to watch, and track whether Merz's retreat converts reform pledges into energy-cost and investment measures that would firm up ACS volumes into 2027.

Süddeutsche Zeitung | Die Zeit | Hürriyet Daily News | Handelsblatt | Initiative Mittelstand

item.title: Canada retaliated with tariffs on C$27.6 billion of US goods and a C$7.5 billion aid package after Washington used a 1930 trade law to impose 50% duties on about USD 28 billion of Canadian goods, as trade talks collapsed over late US demands.
item.description:
The dispute moved from threat to concrete action on both sides. After a near-final deal fell apart, Washington invoked Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act — a rarely used clause letting the president penalise countries deemed to discriminate against US commerce — to put 50% duties on roughly USD 28 billion of Canadian goods, and Trump said tariffs on Canadian cars, trucks, auto parts and steel will rise to 50% from January 2027. On 25 August Canada answered with counter-tariffs on C$27.6 billion (about USD 20 billion) of US goods from 8 September, in tiers of 15%, 25% and 50% across some 700 products: US furniture and clothing face 50%, appliances, dairy and seafood 25%, and machinery, tools and farm equipment 15%. Ottawa added a C$7.5 billion package of loans, liquidity and easier jobless benefits. Both governments blame US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who added last-minute conditions on cars, aluminium quotas and heavy trucks. Ontario threatened to cut electricity exports and restrict critical minerals.

Industry Impact

This is now the central near-term risk for chemical and Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) producers with North American operations. The 50% duties, and a threatened January 2027 jump on autos and steel, raise input costs across the automotive and construction value chains that ACS suppliers serve on both sides of the border, while Canada's 700-product retaliation list — heavy on appliances, machinery, furniture and building inputs — reshapes cross-border flows for those same end-markets. With talks unlikely to resume soon and provinces threatening electricity and critical-mineral curbs, planning certainty is gone. Firms should map exposure on both tariff lists, build pricing and contract flexibility, and watch commodity-export threats that could reach potash and energy feedstocks.

The New York Times | The Straits Times | BNN Bloomberg | Commercial Times | The Globe and Mail | The Daily Mail
